stories.title: Ebola: Artisanal miners keep digging for gold despite virus risk
stories.summary: In eastern Congo, where the economy is heavily dependent on small-scale mining, the constant movement of miners between remote sites is complicating efforts to contain Ebola. Miners in Iga-Barrière are battling the rising cases of Ebola with their need to pay for food and rent. Men and women work for as little as a few dollars a day. Many of them are internally displaced people from a nearby makeshift camp, and have been fleeing conflict for decades. Others come from the surrounding towns and villages. Miner Mechac Ngadjole Katavara, who has lost 13 members of his family, is unable to find medical treatment or vaccinations. "The authorities don't know what to do about this Ebola virus disease,” said Katavara, who is displaced and said he doesn’t have access to disinfectant or other means to protect himself. "We are displaced by war and life is difficult. That is why we have to work under these conditions," he added. Miner Daniel Ndjalenga Musingo, from a town called Ngatsupka, has been working in the Iga-Barrière mine for a month. He said he tried to maintain distance in the mine and not shake hands with others, as he claims the disease is rampant in the villages around the mine. He is asking for the government or the NGOs working to support the response to put an Ebola treatment center in Iga-Barrière.

stories.title: Thousands struggling without power in Indiana 12 days after severe storms
stories.summary: The 77-year-old has been relying on friends to bring her non-perishable food to eat. Her son brought her a power bank so she can charge her phone and keep in touch with the outside world. Thankfully, the summer heat hasn't been too punishing, Dubois said, meaning she has not missed her air conditioning too much. "I've never seen a storm like that in my entire life. Never, never," she tells the BBC. "It was like a sheer wall of wind," she recalls. A wave of sudden, severe storms brought flooding and tornadoes to the US Midwest on 11 August, including to Chicago and Indiana, where seven people were killed. The former industrial town of Gary, which runs along the southern shore of Lake Michigan, was hit particularly hard. Wind gusts peaked at 99mph (159kmh), according to the National Weather Service. The worst of the storm only lasted five to 10 minutes, but the impacts are lingering 12 days later. Power has been restored to more than 345,000 customers since the storm struck, but almost 30,000 were still without power as of Sunday morning, according to the area's electrical company Northern Indiana Public Service Company (Nipsco). In the first few days after the storm, petrol stations, supermarkets and pharmacies were without power, leaving people to survive on what they had.
